title: Google turns to Blue Origin for a rocket, but its long-term problem remains
gist: Blue Origin will launch Google's Project Suncatcher orbital data-center satellites on a New Glenn 7x2 in 2029, but Eric Berger argues Google's real problem is launch dependence: economic space data centers need ~$200/kg launch, likely only achievable by a fully optimized Starship V4, and both SpaceX (Starmind) and Blue Origin (Project Sunrise) are building competing orbital compute constellations.

insights.claim: Blue Origin will launch satellites for Google's Project Suncatcher orbital data center program on a New Glenn 7x2 rocket in 2029, deploying rack-scale compute satellites into Sun-synchronous orbit for near-continuous solar power.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler demand for orbital compute is becoming a real launch-manifest customer category.

insights.claim: The 2029 Suncatcher launch is likely a technology demonstration of networking solar-powered satellites with AI chips and machine-learning compute in space; Google has not disclosed its satellite builder, and satellites may weigh several tons.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Orbital AI compute is still pre-commercial; satellite-builder contract is an open opportunity to watch.

insights.claim: US commercial heavy-lift rockets, including New Glenn, are filling their launch capacity through 2030, making launch slots scarce.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Heavy-lift scarcity gives launch providers pricing power and favors vertically integrated players.
insights.locator: The announcement comes as US commercial heavy lift rockets

insights.claim: Orbital data centers cannot be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers without ultra-low-cost heavy lift; Google planned Suncatcher for the mid-2030s assuming launch costs as low as $200 per kg.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Space-compute economics hinge on launch $/kg — track Starship progress as the key variable.
insights.quote: Without ultra low-cost, heavy lift capability, there is no way that data centers in space can be economically competitive with terrestrial data centers.
insights.locator: There remain a lot of questions about the economic viability

insights.claim: Reaching $200/kg likely requires a fully optimized SpaceX Starship V4 with about 200 metric tons to orbit; SpaceX currently flies Starship V3.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Starship V4 maturity is the single biggest determinant of orbital data center viability.
insights.locator: Upon announcing Project Suncatcher a year ago

insights.claim: SpaceX has spent more than $15 billion developing Starship according to its 2026 securities filings, and both SpaceX and Blue Origin have put over a decade into their large vehicles, making super-heavy-lift entry extremely capital intensive.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: High barriers to entry protect SpaceX/Blue Origin launch duopoly in heavy lift.
insights.locator: But developing a super-heavy-lift rocket requires enormous capital

insights.claim: SpaceX has strong incentives to prioritize its own Starmind orbital data centers on Starship, potentially leaving Google dependent on whatever Starship capacity and pricing SpaceX offers outside customers.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Vertical integration lets SpaceX gatekeep orbital compute — a structural advantage over hyperscalers.

insights.claim: Blue Origin is planning its own orbital data center constellation, Project Sunrise, so Google could end up subsidizing a competitor while paying higher launch costs than Starship offers, since New Glenn 9x4 may be cost-disadvantaged against reusable high-cadence Starship.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Google's launch partnerships transfer value to rivals; expect Google to seek alternative launch access.
insights.quote: So again, Google could be stuck subsidizing a competitor while paying higher launch costs.
insights.locator: Perhaps this explains the new partnership with Blue Origin

insights.claim: Google's options for 2030s launch access are to hope a newer launcher like Rocket Lab, Relativity Space or Stoke Space builds a large rocket and forgoes its own constellation, acquire one of those companies, or build its own rocket program against a 25-year head start.
insights.speaker: Eric Berger
insights.so_what: Raises M&A optionality for Rocket Lab, Relativity or Stoke as hyperscaler acquisition targets.
insights.locator: At this point, Google has some not-great options
